title: Rate of change and real-life graphs

tips.title: The units come off the axes
tips.body: Before working anything out, read the two axes: the gradient is the $y$ unit **per** the $x$ unit, and an area is the $y$ unit **times** it. Litres and minutes give litres per minute for a gradient and litres for an area. That one habit answers most *what does this represent* questions.

tips.title: Average speed is one division
tips.body: $\dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$, with every stopped minute included. Averaging the speeds of the stages is wrong because the stages last different lengths of time — and it is the single most common error in this topic.

tips.title: Less steep is not going down
tips.body: A curve that flattens while still rising means the quantity is **increasing more slowly**, not decreasing. Say which of the two the graph shows before you write your sentence, because the mark is for the distinction.

tips.title: Read a tangent over a long run
tips.body: Take your two points far apart on the tangent — a run of 4 rather than 0.5. The line is drawn by eye, so a small slip in reading is unavoidable; a long run makes it barely matter, while a short run multiplies it.

why.matters:
On any graph of one thing against another, the **gradient is a rate** and the **area is a total**. Those two facts are the whole topic, and between them they turn a picture into numbers.

What makes it worth the effort is that the rate is usually the thing you actually care about and the thing nobody measured. Nobody records acceleration; they record speed against time. Nobody records how fast a tank fills; they record depth. The gradient is how you get from what was measured to what was meant.

examples.title: What the two halves of a graph mean
examples.body:
A train pulls away, reaching 30 m/s after 10 seconds, then holds that speed for 20 more.

The gradient of the first part is the acceleration: 30 over 10, which is 3 m/s². The second part is flat, so the gradient is 0 — no acceleration, which is not the same as not moving, and that is the distinction the question is usually testing.

The area is the distance. Under the sloping part it is a triangle, $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 30 = 150$ m. Under the flat part it is a rectangle, 20 × 30 = 600 m. Altogether 750 m in 30 seconds.

And that checks out: 750 over 30 is 25 m/s average, which is between 0 and 30 as it has to be. Every speed camera, fitness tracker and flight recorder in the world is doing this — reading a rate off a slope and a total off an area.

visual.alt: A speed against time graph rising in a straight line from rest to thirty metres per second over ten seconds and then flat for twenty more, with the area beneath it shaded

steps.title: The gradient is a rate
steps.body:
On a real-life graph the **gradient means something**, and what it means comes from the axes:

$$\text{gradient} = \frac{\text{change in the } y \text{ value}}{\text{change in the } x \text{ value}} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$$

If $y$ is distance in km and $x$ is time in hours, the gradient is km per hour — a **speed**. If $y$ is the volume in a tank in litres and $x$ is time in minutes, the gradient is litres per minute — a **flow rate**.

So the units of the gradient are always **the $y$ unit per the $x$ unit**, and reading them off the axes tells you what the number is before you have worked anything out.

Three things follow, and they cover most of the topic:

- A **steeper** line means a **faster** rate.
- A **horizontal** line means the gradient is zero: nothing is changing.
- A **downward** slope means a **negative** rate — the quantity is falling.

steps.title: Reading a distance–time graph
steps.body:
On a **distance–time** graph, the gradient is the **speed**. A journey with stages shows as a line with corners, and each straight section has its own speed.

A **horizontal** section means the distance is not changing — the object has **stopped**.

steps.title: Average speed is not the average of the speeds
steps.body:
In the journey above the car drove at 60 km/h, stopped, then drove at 60 km/h again — but the **average speed for the whole journey was 50 km/h**.

That is not a trick. Average speed always means

$$\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$$

and the total time includes every minute spent stopped. Here it is $\frac{150}{3} = 50$ km/h.

The common error is to average the speeds instead: $\frac{60 + 0 + 60}{3} = 40$, which is wrong, because the three stages **took different lengths of time**. The half hour stopped should not count as much as the hour and a half driving.

On the graph, the average speed is the gradient of the **straight line from the start of the journey to the end** — one line drawn across all the corners. That picture is worth holding on to: if someone asks for average speed, they are asking for a single gradient from the first point to the last.

And if the question asks for the average speed **while moving**, exclude the stop: $\frac{150}{2.5} = 60$ km/h.

steps.title: Velocity–time graphs: gradient and area
steps.body:
A **velocity–time** graph carries two pieces of information, and questions ask for both:

- the **gradient** is the **acceleration**, in m/s per second, written m/s²;
- the **area under the graph** is the **distance travelled**.

The area is the part students forget. It works because distance is speed × time, which is exactly what an area under a velocity–time graph measures.

steps.title: A curve: the rate is changing
steps.body:
When the graph is a **curve**, the rate is different at every moment — that is what the curve is telling you. Water cools quickly at first and then more slowly, so the graph is steep at the start and flattens out.

To find the rate **at one instant**, draw a **tangent**: a straight line that just touches the curve at that point, and find its gradient.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.** A cyclist's distance–time graph goes $(0, 0)$ to $(0.5, 10)$, then $(0.5, 10)$ to $(1, 10)$, then $(1, 10)$ to $(2, 34)$, with distance in km and time in hours.

5. Find the acceleration in the first 5 seconds.
6. Find the total distance travelled.

**Part C.**

7. A tank is filling. Its volume–time graph is a curve that gets **less** steep. Describe in words what is happening to the flow rate, and say how you would estimate it at 4 minutes.

steps.title: Going deeper: describing a graph, and what the area means
steps.body:
**Say what the gradient means, not just what it is.** A question that says *interpret the gradient* wants a sentence in the context of the question: not *the gradient is 3* but **the tank is filling at 3 litres per minute**. Naming the quantity and the units is what earns the mark.

**Curves, in words.** The shape tells a story, and there are only a few:

- Getting **steeper** — the rate is **increasing**: filling faster and faster.
- Getting **less steep** — the rate is **decreasing**, but the quantity is still rising.
- **Flattening towards a level** — approaching a limit: a cooling drink reaching room temperature, a tank reaching full.
- **Horizontal** — nothing is changing at all.

The distinction in the second one matters. *The volume is decreasing* and *the volume is increasing more slowly* are different statements, and a curve that flattens while still rising means the second.

**The area under a graph is a quantity too.** Its meaning is the $y$ unit **times** the $x$ unit, just as the gradient was one **per** the other:

- velocity (m/s) × time (s) = **distance** (m);
- flow rate (litres/min) × time (min) = **volume** (litres);
- power (kW) × time (hours) = **energy** (kWh).

So asking what an area means is the same trick as asking what a gradient means: look at the axes.

**Estimating an area under a curve.** Split the region into strips — trapeziums or triangles and rectangles — work out each, and add. It is an **estimate**, and you should say whether it is an over- or under-estimate: if the curve bulges **above** the straight tops of your trapeziums, the trapezium rule **under**estimates.

**On tangents.** Draw the tangent long, and take your two points **far apart** on it. A tangent read over a run of 0.5 turns a small slip in reading into a large error in the gradient; read over a run of 4 and the same slip barely shows.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The **gradient** of a real-life graph is a **rate**, and its units are the $y$ unit **per** the $x$ unit.
- $\text{gradient} = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$, read from two points as far apart as possible.
- On a **distance–time** graph the gradient is **speed**; a horizontal section means **stopped**.
- **Average speed** $= \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$ — never the average of the speeds.
- On a **velocity–time** graph the gradient is **acceleration** and the **area** is **distance**.
- The **area** under a graph means the $y$ unit **times** the $x$ unit.
- A **curve** means the rate is changing: steeper is faster, flatter is slower.
- For the rate at an instant, draw a **tangent** and find its gradient — an estimate, so say *about*.
- Less steep but still rising means **increasing more slowly**, not decreasing.
- *Interpret* means write a sentence with the quantity and the units in it.

questions.prompt: What does the gradient of a distance–time graph tell you?
questions.solution: Distance divided by time is speed, so the gradient of a distance–time graph is the speed.

questions.prompt: What does a horizontal section of a distance–time graph mean?
questions.solution: The distance is not changing, so the gradient is zero: the object has **stopped**.

questions.prompt: A graph has volume in litres against time in minutes. What are the units of the gradient?
questions.solution: The gradient is always the $y$ unit **per** the $x$ unit: litres per minute.

questions.solution: Velocity divided by time is acceleration, in m/s per second.

questions.solution: While moving: $\dfrac{150}{2.5} = 60$ km/h. Over the whole journey it would be $\dfrac{150}{3} = 50$ km/h — read which the question wants.

questions.prompt: A velocity–time graph rises in a straight line from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, 12)$, stays level at 12 m/s until $t = 10$, then falls in a straight line to $(14, 0)$. Velocity is in m/s and time in seconds. Find the acceleration in the first 4 seconds, the acceleration in the last 4 seconds, and the total distance travelled.
questions.solution: The acceleration is the gradient of the graph. In the first four seconds the velocity rises from zero to twelve metres per second, so the gradient is twelve divided by four, which is three metres per second squared. In the last four seconds the velocity falls from twelve metres per second to zero, so the gradient is minus twelve divided by four, which is minus three metres per second squared, a deceleration of three metres per second squared. The total distance is the area under the graph. The shape is a trapezium with parallel sides of fourteen seconds and six seconds and a height of twelve metres per second, so the area is a half of fourteen plus six, all multiplied by twelve, which is one hundred and twenty metres. This can be checked by splitting the shape into a triangle of area twenty four metres, a rectangle of area seventy two metres and a second triangle of area twenty four metres, which add to one hundred and twenty metres.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Acceleration is the gradient.**

First 4 seconds, from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, 12)$:

$$a = \frac{12 - 0}{4 - 0} = 3 \text{ m/s}^2$$

Last 4 seconds, from $(10, 12)$ to $(14, 0)$:

$$a = \frac{0 - 12}{14 - 10} = -3 \text{ m/s}^2$$

The minus sign means it is **decelerating** at 3 m/s². Say so — the sign is part of the answer.

**Distance is the area.** The shape is a trapezium with parallel sides 14 and 6 and height 12:

$$\text{area} = \frac{14 + 6}{2} \times 12 = 120 \text{ m}$$

**Check by splitting it up:**

- triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 12 = 24$
- rectangle: $6 \times 12 = 72$
- triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 12 = 24$

$24 + 72 + 24 = 120$ m ✓

Two methods agreeing is the strongest check available here, and it costs two lines.

questions.prompt: A cup of tea cools from 90 °C. Its temperature–time graph is a curve that falls steeply at first and then flattens towards 50 °C. Explain what the shape tells you about the rate of cooling, and describe how you would estimate the rate of cooling at 3 minutes.
questions.solution: The graph is steep at the start, which means the temperature is falling quickly at first. As time goes on the curve becomes less steep, so the gradient is smaller and the tea is still cooling but more and more slowly. The curve flattens towards fifty degrees, which suggests the tea is approaching the temperature of the room and will not cool below it, so the rate of cooling approaches zero. To estimate the rate of cooling at three minutes I would draw a tangent to the curve at the point where the time is three minutes, using a ruler so that the line just touches the curve there. I would then choose two points on the tangent that are far apart, read their coordinates, and work out the gradient as the change in temperature divided by the change in time. The answer would be negative because the temperature is falling, and it would be an estimate because the tangent is drawn by eye.

questions.modelAnswer:
**What the shape says.**

- **Steep at the start**: the tea is cooling **quickly** — the biggest temperature drop happens in the first minute or two.
- **Getting less steep**: the gradient is shrinking, so the tea is **still cooling but more slowly**. Note the distinction: the temperature is going down throughout; it is the *rate* that is falling.
- **Flattening towards 50 °C**: the tea is approaching **room temperature**, and the rate of cooling approaches zero. It will not cool below the room.

**Estimating the rate at 3 minutes.**

1. Draw a **tangent** at the point where $t = 3$ — a ruled line that just touches the curve there, not a chord across it.
2. Read **two points far apart** on the tangent, such as $(1, 68)$ and $(5, 44)$.
3. Gradient $= \dfrac{44 - 68}{5 - 1} = -6$.

So the tea is cooling at about **6 °C per minute** at that moment. The answer is **negative** because the temperature is falling, and it is an **estimate** because the tangent is drawn by eye — which is why reading two points far apart matters.

examTechnique.body:
Read the axes first, including the units, and decide what a gradient and an area would each mean before doing any arithmetic.

For a gradient, pick two points that are far apart and ideally on grid intersections, then write rise over run with the numbers in it. Showing the fraction is a method mark even if the division goes wrong.

On a distance–time graph, a flat section means stopped. On a velocity–time graph, remember the area as well as the gradient — questions ask for both.

For average speed, write total distance over total time. Check whether the question means the whole journey or only the time moving.

For a curve, draw the tangent with a ruler and read two widely spaced points on it. Answers are accepted over a range, so give the value and say *about*.

When a question says interpret or describe, write a sentence naming the quantity and its units: not *3*, but *the tank fills at 3 litres per minute*.
examinerErrors: Averaging the speeds of the stages instead of dividing total distance by total time.
Leaving the stopped time out of the total when the question asks for the whole journey.
Giving a gradient with no units, or with the units the wrong way round.
Reading the gradient of a chord instead of drawing a tangent.
Taking two tangent points very close together, so a small reading error becomes a large one.
Saying a quantity is decreasing when the curve is only becoming less steep.
Forgetting that the area under a velocity–time graph is the distance.
Writing a bare number when the question asked for an interpretation in context.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer reads the axes before anything else, so it knows the gradient is litres per minute and the area is litres without being told. It quotes rise over run with the numbers in, which protects the method mark. It never averages speeds. On a curve it draws the tangent with a ruler and reads two points far apart, then says *about*, because it understands why the answer is an estimate. It distinguishes *decreasing* from *increasing more slowly*, which is the sentence most answers get wrong. And when asked to interpret, it writes a sentence with the quantity and the units in it rather than leaving a naked number for the examiner to interpret.
